About me

I am presently a computer science graduate student at Cornell University. My research interests lie broadly in building trustworthy computer systems. Problems relating to formal specifications, security, extensibility and programmability appeal to me in particular. I am fortunate to be advised by Andrew Myers and Robbert van Renesse to pursue my interests. Before making the questionable decision to become a grad student, I had a blast as an undergrad at IIT Roorkee, where I was awarded the director's gold medal. On the internet, my accounts usually have a character from the greatest show ever.

Research

We can only build secure and trustworthy systems if we know what secure and trustworthy means. In a nutshell, my research is about finding and enforcing the right specifications for computer systems. I'm currently working on the following projects:

Real–ideal semantic foundations for language-based security

Existing security properties such as noninterference are too simplistic; they cannot capture the security requirements of practical systems, which often have intertwined confidentiality and integrity requirements. Our insight is to adapt the real–ideal paradigm from cryptography to give simple and expressive security specifications for computer systems. This has been quite successful. Using this paradigm, we have been able to provide simple semantic definitions of important—but less understood—security properties (such as nonmalleable information flow, robust declassification, and confused deputy attack security). In fact, we show that even syntactic type soundness theorems for information-flow type systems are presented best as real–ideal statements.

Joint work with Andrew Myers, Silei Ren, and Hanxi Chen.

Enforcing auditable specifications for AI prompts

Using AI is exhilarating. Its lack of guarantees is also terrifying. The right interaction model with AI must be to combine LLM prompting with techniques from programming languages and formal methods. We are designing simple, easily auditable, refinable, and enforceable specification languages to constrain AI execution to give users functionality and security guarantees. Moreover, AI can itself generate such specifications, lifting significant user burden; a user only needs to audit the generated specification. Additionally, AI's remarkable ability to write formal proofs can even automate specification refinement! Such an interaction model is an important step in a future where we use our AI superpowers more responsibly. Because, with great power comes great responsibility.

Joint work with Andrew Myers, Alexandra Silva, and Guy Amir.

Self-managing chain replication

The original chain replication protocol has been in use in many companies and research projects. One downside of chain replication is that it cannot stand on its own and requires a configuration service. It turns out that this is not fundamental: a chain replicated service can reconfigure itself, for example after a failure. The new protocol also addresses certain inefficiencies in the original protocol, such as latency increasing with chain length.

Joint work with Robbert van Renesse, Fred Schneider, and Yacqub Mohamed.
